clue.text: Poem about shop girl, third class, say

indicators.note: about means moved around, so these letters are jumbled into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
a C is a third-class grade, after A and B
taken as written

explanation.surface: A poem concerning a girl who works in a shop and has had a third-rate education.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' shuffles SHOPGIRL + C + SAY. 'say' looks like a link word meaning 'for example' but its letters are part of the anagram. The title is Matthew Arnold's 'The Scholar-Gipsy', the puzzle's theme poet.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a pastoral elegy by Matthew Arnold about an Oxford student who joined travelling Roma.

clue.text: Herb sap.?

explanation.surface: A plant clue reduced to a mysterious abbreviation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sap.' is short for Latin 'sapiens', wise, as in Homo sapiens; the question mark flags the leap from the abbreviation to the noun meaning a wise man.
explanation.definitionFit: A culinary plant of the mint family, and a wise person, the Latin 'sapiens' being the source of the abbreviation.

clue.text: Hands apology (sic) over to Western hero

indicators.note: over here means turned over or knocked about, so the letters are reworked

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone hands over an apology, with a 'sic' noting an error, to a cowboy star.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracketed 'sic' reads as an editor's note but is simply three more letters of the anagram fodder; 'over' tells you to rearrange HANDS + APOLOGY + SIC.
explanation.definitionFit: This cowboy character appeared in novels by Clarence Mulford and in many Western films.

clue.text: Format relating to the 22?

explanation.surface: A design term somehow connected with the departed.
explanation.walkthrough: 22 is DEAD. To lay out a corpse is to prepare it for burial, so the second sense reads the answer as a verb phrase applied to the dead.
explanation.definitionFit: Arrangement or format of a page, and laying out a body: preparing the dead for burial.

clue.text: Island ways as reported

indicators.note: as reported means as heard spoken, so the word is replaced by one sounding the same

parts.note: ways are roads

explanation.surface: Someone describes the routes on a Mediterranean island as told to them.
explanation.definitionFit: A large Greek island in the Dodecanese, once home to the Colossus.

clue.text: Old club gets a lot of support

indicators.note: a lot of means most but not all, so the end is dropped from the word

parts.note: a brassiere is a support garment

explanation.surface: A vintage golfing team receives plenty of backing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a lot of' trims the last two letters RE off BRASSIERE. 'gets' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: An early wooden golf club, roughly equivalent to a modern two-wood, now obsolete.

clue.text: Commonplace quality got by including gossip with literature

indicators.note: including means the word by holds the other pieces inside it

parts.note: ana is a collection of anecdotes or table talk about a person

explanation.surface: Ordinariness arises when you add tittle-tattle to books.
explanation.walkthrough: ANA, a collection of gossip or sayings about someone, is a crossword favourite. 'got' and 'with' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: Being trite and unoriginal is the quality of the commonplace, which is a synonym for this noun.

clue.text: Flying first into tree on Tyneside

indicators.note: on means placed after, so the region follows in a down clue
into means the first piece goes inside the tree word

parts.note: arbor is Latin for tree
I is the Roman numeral one, the first
Tyneside is in the North East of England, abbreviated NE

explanation.surface: Something takes off first into a tree in the north of England.
explanation.walkthrough: Arbor is Latin for tree and the American spelling of arbour; Tyneside, around Newcastle, is in north-east England.
explanation.definitionFit: Something airborne is aloft and moving through the air, which is what flying means.

clue.text: Poem all about zero hour for a group with effect of disuse

indicators.note: about means the word all goes around everything else

parts.note: a sum is the whole amount, all of it
O looks like zero
a band is a group of musicians
rust forms on metal left unused

explanation.surface: A poem concerning the moment of action for a band that has gone rusty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'zero hour' looks like one phrase but splits into two pieces. 'for' and 'with' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: This narrative poem by Matthew Arnold tells of a Persian warrior unknowingly killing his son.

clue.text: Poem edited to suit Long John recited on a volcano

indicators.note: to suit means adapted to fit, so the letters are reshaped

parts.note: taken as written: its four letters are anagram fodder

indicators.note: recited means spoken, so the name is swapped for its sound

parts.note: the comedian John Cleese is famously tall

explanation.surface: A poem revised for a tall man to recite on a volcano.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to suit' rearranges POEM + ED into EMPEDO; 'recited' turns tall comic John Cleese's name into its sound. Arnold's poem is 'Empedocles on Etna', so the answer plus 'on a volcano' names it.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek philosopher was said to have died by leaping into Etna, so his story ends on a volcano.

clue.text: See 1
Queen in leaderless municipality takes possession

indicators.note: in means the queen goes inside the shortened word
leaderless means the first letter is dropped

parts.note: a township is a municipality
ER stands for Elizabeth Regina, the queen

explanation.surface: A monarch in a headless town seizes control of property.
explanation.walkthrough: 'takes' is a link; the definition is the single word at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Owning something is having it as a possession, so the two nouns are synonyms.

clue.text: Spotted climber reprising cup role, a doddle

indicators.note: reprising means going over again in a new form, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Playing a cup-final part again proves very easy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reprising' rearranges CUP ROLE A DODDLE. 'Spotted climber' suggests a plant or a mountaineer seen somewhere, but means a tree-climbing cat with blotched markings.
explanation.definitionFit: This Asian wild cat has cloud-shaped markings and is an expert tree climber.

clue.text: Virtually the same horse after reindeer man's following leader

indicators.note: after means the horse comes after the altered name
following leader means the first letter is replaced by the letter after it in the alphabet

parts.note: Santa Claus is the man with the reindeer
a mount is a horse to ride

explanation.surface: A horse trails behind Father Christmas's team leader.
explanation.walkthrough: 'following leader' looks like a position but asks for the letter after the leader in the alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: Tantamount means equivalent in effect, so something nearly identical in value is virtually the same.

clue.text: Poems' author dropping would flower in Italy

indicators.note: dropping means the contraction is taken out of the name

parts.note: Matthew Arnold wrote the poems in this puzzle
'ld is an old contraction of would, as in Shakespeare's I'ld

explanation.surface: A poet stops versifying and becomes something growing in Italy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flower' is a river (something that flows), not a bloom. ARNOLD loses LD, an archaic short form of 'would'.
explanation.definitionFit: The river running through Florence and Pisa: a flower in the crossword sense of something that flows.

clue.text: Street fighter from down under captures one like 1 9 or 25 rather than 7 or 19 22

indicators.note: captures means the soldier holds the numeral inside

parts.note: an Anzac is an Australian or New Zealand soldier
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: An Australian soldier in the street seizes someone similar to certain poems.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Scholar-Gipsy' and 'Thyrsis' are written in stanzas; 'Sohrab and Rustum' and 'Balder Dead' are blank verse.
explanation.definitionFit: Stanzaic means written in stanzas, the regular verse groups of those two poems.

clue.text: It's sweet and slow time for girls

parts.note: a mo is a moment, a short time
lasses are girls

explanation.surface: A slow, tender moment spent with young women.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for' is a link. 'Slow as molasses' is a stock phrase, so the definition covers the syrup's slowness too.
explanation.definitionFit: This thick dark syrup from sugar refining is sweet and proverbially slow to pour.

clue.text: Guns providing back-to-back text

indicators.note: back means read the word backwards

parts.note: providing means if
the rear is the back
MS is a manuscript, a written text

explanation.surface: Weapons that supply messages sent in both directions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back-to-back' looks like one idea but splits into two backs: the first a reversal signal, the second a synonym. 'to' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Firearms are guns and other weapons that shoot bullets.

clue.text: Sleuth with refresher on a plate

parts.note: tec is short for detective, a sleuth
a tonic is a refreshing drink or pick-me-up

explanation.surface: A detective with a drink served on a dish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on a plate' suggests something easy or served up, but refers to the plates of the Earth's crust. 'with' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Tectonic describes movement of the Earth's crustal plates, hence relating to what happens on a plate.

clue.text: The advantageous side

parts.note: a side or rim that is also a slight lead over a rival

explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a side or border and an advantage, so it combines the two senses.

clue.text: Poem, not good, about tree and some deities

indicators.note: about means the bad word goes around the tree and the fragment

parts.note: bad means not good
an alder is a tree

indicators.note: some means only part of the word deities is used

explanation.surface: A poor poem about a tree and several gods.
explanation.walkthrough: 'some' takes only the start of 'deities', which with the tree goes inside the word for not good.
explanation.definitionFit: This poem by Matthew Arnold retells the Norse myth of the death of the god Balder.

clue.text: A little bit of Wales is where the Queen Mother was

parts.note: Glam is a short form of Glamorgan, a Welsh county
taken as written

explanation.surface: A small part of Wales is where a royal grandmother lived.
explanation.walkthrough: Glamorgan is a historic county of south Wales; 'little' signals its shortened form GLAM.
explanation.definitionFit: Glamis Castle in Scotland was the childhood home of Elizabeth Bowes-Lyon, later the Queen Mother.

clue.text: Service time followed by old talker, say: there's the rub

parts.note: Mass is a church service
an age is a period of time

indicators.note: say means spoken aloud, so a word with the same sound is used

parts.note: parleur is Old French for a talker or speaker

explanation.surface: After church comes a long while with a chatterbox, and there lies the difficulty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'there's the rub' is Hamlet's phrase for a snag, here read literally as a place for rubbing. 'followed by' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A place offering massages is literally where rubbing happens, so Hamlet's phrase for a problem doubles as its description.

clue.text: See 19
Nude's ruin (ruined because not covered)

indicators.note: ruined means wrecked, so the preceding letters are broken up and rebuilt

explanation.surface: A naked person's downfall happens because they had no insurance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'because' is a link; 'ruined' rearranges NUDES RUIN, which are printed inside the brackets.
explanation.definitionFit: To have no insurance is to have no cover, so not covered is a synonym.

clue.text: Joint head of church comes under it

definitions.text: head of church comes under it

explanation.surface: A connection that a church leader's head sits beneath.
explanation.walkthrough: A mitre joint is a carpentry corner joint; a bishop, a head of the church, wears the tall hat called a mitre.
explanation.definitionFit: A woodworking corner joint at 45 degrees, and the tall ceremonial hat a bishop wears.

clue.text: Poem is on solver's rights

indicators.note: on means placed after, so the word is follows the other pieces

parts.note: thy is an old word for your, the solver's
R is right, so RS is rights
taken as written

explanation.surface: A poem about the reader's entitlements.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue speaks to the solver, so 'solver's' means 'your', archaically THY.
explanation.definitionFit: Arnold's elegy for his friend Arthur Hugh Clough, a sequel to his Oxford pastoral.

clue.text: Started again having grass about half the season

indicators.note: about means the grass goes around the fragment

parts.note: a reed is a tall grass

indicators.note: half means only the first half of the word is used

parts.note: summer is a season

explanation.surface: Someone took up work again with reeds around for part of the summer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'having' is a link; 'half' takes the first three letters of the season.
explanation.definitionFit: To resume is to begin again after a pause.
